name: Northeast Couloir
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FS Road 7601 (Eightmile Road), elevation ~3,400 ft — in early season when Eightmile Road is gated/snowed in, tack on roughly 4 additional miles of road walking/skiing from the Bridge Creek Campground area on Icicle Road. From the trailhead, follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles and 1,100 ft of gain to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail forks right (south); the Stuart Lake Trail continues straight to Stuart Lake/Colchuck Pass and is not your route. Climb the steep, rooty switchbacks of the Colchuck Lake Trail through boulder fields for another 1.6 miles and 1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4 miles and 2,200 ft from the car) — this is the only reliable water source below the basin, and it's your last easy resupply. Pick up the boot path along the lake's east shore (the west side is brushier and slower) to the inlet at the south end (~5 miles in). Leave the maintained trail here and ascend talus, heather benches, or lingering snow (highly season-dependent) up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft. Rather than heading up-glacier toward Colchuck/Banshee Col (that's the Colchuck Glacier route), traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the main fall line under the north face and Northeast Buttress to limit rockfall and icefall exposure. The Northeast Couloir's entrance is the obvious narrow slot splitting the north face just east of the Northeast Buttress; gaining it typically requires crossing a moat at the glacier's edge, which varies from a simple step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer. Expect avalanche-prone slopes above the lake in spring/early-summer conditions, and increasing rockfall down the couloir itself as the day warms.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction and fork right for Colchuck Lake — straight on goes to Stuart Lake and a different valley. Switchback up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles and 2,200 ft in, and fill water: it is the last easy source. Take the boot path along the lake's east shore, which is faster than the west, to the inlet at the south end. Leave the trail there and climb talus, heather benches or snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Now the important part. Do not continue up-glacier toward the col — that is the Colchuck Glacier route. Traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the fall line under the face. If Eightmile Road is gated in early season, add roughly four miles of road each way.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow and ice climb; by high summer the entry moat opens and the couloir sheds rock
hazards: Rockfall down the couloir once the sun reaches the face
An entry moat that can require an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer
Avalanche-prone slopes above Colchuck Lake in spring and early summer
Steep snow and ice to 60-plus degrees at the exit
Reversing the couloir is discouraged — plan on the Colchuck Glacier walk-off, which is long
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The couloirs come in order, and counting them is the test. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier along its true-right margin you pass features in a fixed sequence, and this one is the second deep slot you meet, not the first.

Lowest on the glacier: the North Buttress Couloir. Above it, and starting with two rope-lengths of ice below a hidden couloir: the Holsten-Hilden. Higher up the glacier than either: the Northeast Couloir — the one you want. Above and south of it: the rock of the Northeast Buttress.

So the paired check is slot-and-rib. You are correct when you are standing in an obvious narrow slot splitting the face, with the prominent rock buttress immediately to your south. If the buttress is not there, you are too low on the glacier. If you are scrambling onto the toe of that rock rather than into a slot, you are on the Northeast Buttress and on a fourteen-pitch rock route instead of a snow and ice one.

The moat is part of the arrival, not an obstacle before it: gaining the couloir means crossing the moat at the glacier's edge, and it runs from a step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by late summer. If you reach rock with no moat to cross at all, you have probably reached it somewhere it is filled and should confirm the slot above you before committing.

What it does above, as confirmation: the couloir winds up, steepens, and runs into a steep wall. The exit is along the base of that wall to the climber's left, finishing on 60-plus degree snow or ice to the summit ridge. A couloir that simply keeps going without hitting a wall is not this one.
